lead: Zone 2 cardio is low-to-moderate intensity steady aerobic exercise, the second band in popular five-zone heart-rate schemes, often described as a pace at which conversation is still possible. It is used by people who want to lean out and improve conditioning without the fatigue of hard intervals: easy sessions of walking, cycling, rowing, swimming or jogging burn calories, lean on fat as the main fuel and leave energy for lifting, so they can be added to a physique plan without eating into recovery.[1]

Wikipedia's aerobic exercise article describes repeated light-to-moderate activity over extended periods, with fat and glycogen as the main fuels and relatively more fat used at lower intensity.[1] Endurance training also drives mitochondrial biogenesis, in which energy depletion activates AMPK and the regulator PGC-1 alpha, raising the muscle's oxidative capacity over time.[2]

The 'Zone 2' name has no single standard definition: heart-rate zones can be built from a percentage of maximum heart rate, from heart rate reserve (the Karvonen method) or from fixed offsets below maximum (the Zoladz method).[3] No published trial has tested Zone 2 as a named protocol for appearance.

chain: Calories burned with fat as a main fuel and low recovery cost

angle.text: Zone 2 sessions add energy expenditure and aerobic fitness at an intensity easy enough to sit alongside weight training. Over weeks they support a leaner look and better work capacity for training.

infobox: Brisk walking, easy cycling, swimming, jogging[1]
Conversational pace; heart-rate zone defined several ways[3]

paras: Aerobic exercise guidance recommends about 2.5 hours a week of moderate activity to lower health risks, and even about 11 minutes a day has been associated with lower risk of early death, with high-intensity interval training possibly giving similar benefits in less time.[1]

Training intensity can be written as a percentage of maximum heart rate. Wikipedia notes that the common 220-minus-age estimate was not derived from original research and can be off by about 24 beats per minute for an individual at the 95 percent level, so zones set from it are approximate; a supervised maximal test is the most accurate method.[3] Under the Zoladz method, zones are set from maximum heart rate minus fixed adjusters, with zone 1 for a maximum of 180 about 125 to 135 beats per minute.[3]

At lower intensities the body relies mainly on fat, shifting toward glycogen as intensity rises; the same source notes that low-to-moderate exercise burns fewer calories per unit time than high-intensity exercise.[1]

A training table on Wikipedia's endurance training page lists 'extensive basic endurance' sessions, with lactate clearly below the aerobic threshold, as aimed at health, endurance and fat metabolism, and long-term endurance training is described as lowering resting heart rate and raising stroke volume and cardiac output.[4] Endurance exercise also stimulates mitochondrial biogenesis through AMPK and PGC-1 alpha signalling.[2]

sections.h: Use in physique and looksmaxxing communities
paras: Zone 2 sessions are discussed as a way to add cardio during a cut without hard intervals, and as a way to build the aerobic base that supports faster recovery between sets. Strength-training logs on forums such as T Nation commonly mention easy cardio alongside lifting.
No studies found specific to Zone 2 as a named protocol. General evidence on aerobic exercise is summarised under its own topic.[1]

name: Zone 2 cardio

card.summary: Easy, steady cardio at conversational pace; popular, but little zone-specific research for appearance goals.
card.note: Sources reviewed contain no trials of Zone 2 as such.

quick.overview:
Zone 2 is steady, easy-to-moderate cardio, usually measured by heart rate or the ability to talk.

It is widely promoted for fat use and endurance, but the sources reviewed do not include trials of Zone 2 as a named method.
quick.mechanism: Low intensity relies mostly on fat for fuel, with more glycogen used as intensity rises.
quick.risks: General aerobic exercise is considered low-risk; people with health conditions are generally advised to consult a clinician.
